missing.fix: Fill it in, or ask for a suggestion. You can save a draft, but the story can't be generated until it is filled.

not_allowed.message: {label} has a value that isn't one of the choices.
not_allowed.fix: Pick one of the listed choices.

too_many.fix: Remove an item or merge similar ones.

invalid.message: {label} has a value that can't be used.
invalid.fix: Check the entry and try again.

style.label: Style
style.summary: How the story is told: voice, attitude and the narrator's habit of attention. It names no people, places or plot, so it can be used with any story.

groups.label: Narration
groups.help: Fixed rules for the whole story.

groups.label: Narrator
groups.help: How close, how funny and how fast the telling is.

groups.label: Sentences and words
groups.help: How the prose sounds on the page.

groups.label: Stance
groups.help: The narrator's attitude toward the story.

groups.label: Dialogue
groups.help: How people talk to each other.

groups.label: Genre and lens
groups.help: Two free-text levers with a big effect.

fields.label: Person
fields.help: Whose voice tells the story. This is a rule for every chapter, and the protagonist you pick in Setup must fit it.
fields.why: It changes every sentence, so it is fixed for the whole story and Setup checks your protagonist against it.

options.label: First person
options.description: “I walked in and the room went quiet.”

options.label: Third person
options.description: “She walked in and the room went quiet.”

fields.label: Tense
fields.help: Past reads like a story being told. Present feels immediate. Applies to every chapter.
fields.why: Fixed for every chapter, so pick the one you can live with for the whole story.

options.label: Past
options.description: “He opened the door.”

options.label: Present
options.description: “He opens the door.”

fields.label: Distance
fields.help: How far the narrator stands from the protagonist's thoughts.
fields.why: Decides how much of the protagonist's inner life the reader gets.

options.label: External
options.description: “She read the letter twice. She folded it and put it on the table.”

options.label: Close
options.description: “She read the letter twice. It couldn't be true, and she knew it was.”

options.label: Deep
options.description: “Twice through, and the words would not settle. His handwriting. His coat still on the chair. It could not be true.”

fields.label: Humor
fields.help: How much the telling jokes, and what kind.
fields.why: Sets whether the reader is invited to laugh at what happens.

options.label: None
options.description: No jokes. The tone stays serious.

options.label: Dry
options.description: “The meeting ran long, in the way the Ice Age ran long.”

options.label: Absurd
options.description: “The goat had been appointed treasurer, and nobody saw reason to object.”

options.label: Dark
options.description: “The funeral was well attended, which was more than he had managed in life.”

fields.label: Pacing
fields.help: How quickly the telling moves. Faster is generally easier to enjoy.
fields.why: Decides how much page each moment gets, so it also shapes how long chapters run.

options.label: Lingering
options.description: A scene can spend a page on a doorway.

options.label: Balanced
options.description: Slows down for what matters and skips the rest.

options.label: Brisk
options.description: Scenes start late, end early and rarely stop to look around.

fields.label: Narrator note
fields.help: Anything else about the narrator. Passed to the model exactly as you write it.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Knows more than it tells; sometimes speaks to the reader.

fields.label: Rhythm
fields.help: How sentences sound.
fields.why: Sentence length sets the pace of reading, line by line.

options.label: Terse
options.description: “She ran. The door slammed. Nothing.”

options.label: Varied
options.description: “She ran. Down the stairs, past the landing where the light always failed, and out before the door finished closing.”

options.label: Flowing
options.description: “She ran down the stairs and past the landing where the light always failed and out through the door that was still swinging closed behind her.”

fields.label: Diction
fields.help: Word choice: everyday or elaborate.
fields.why: Plain words keep the reader moving; ornate ones make them slow down and notice the language.

options.label: Plain
options.description: “The room was cold and smelled of damp.”

options.label: Ornate
options.description: “The chamber held a cold older than the house, and the damp breathed from the plaster like a held grievance.”

fields.label: Register
fields.help: How formal the narration sounds.
fields.why: Sets whether the narrator sounds like a person talking to you or a record being kept.

options.label: Formal
options.description: “He declined the offer, as the circumstances required.”

options.label: Casual
options.description: “He turned it down. Didn't really have a choice.”

fields.label: Imagery
fields.help: How much figurative language the prose uses.
fields.why: More figurative language means more texture and slower reading.

options.label: Literal
options.description: “The wind was strong and cold.”

options.label: Occasional
options.description: “The wind was cold, and it pushed at her as if it wanted something.”

options.label: Lush
options.description: “The wind came off the water in long silver sheets, cold as a knife laid flat against the skin.”

fields.label: Edge
fields.help: Language strength: swearing, bluntness, roughness.
fields.why: Decides whether rough events are narrated in rough language.

options.label: Clean
options.description: “Get out,” she said. “I mean it.”

options.label: Coarse
options.description: “Get the hell out,” she said. “I mean it, damn you.”

fields.label: Explicitness
fields.help: Whether intense moments (violence, intimacy) happen on the page or just off it.
fields.why: Decides what the reader sees directly and what they have to imagine.

options.label: Implied
options.description: The door closes on the worst of it, and the next scene starts after.

options.label: Shown
options.description: The worst of it happens in front of the reader, in plain detail.

fields.label: Sentences and words note
fields.help: Anything else about the prose. Passed to the model exactly as you write it.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Avoid semicolons; favour concrete nouns.

fields.label: Attitude
fields.help: The narrator's feeling toward the story and its people.
fields.why: The narrator's feeling shows in what it notices and how it words the same event.

options.label: Earnest
options.description: “He missed the train, and it mattered: she would be waiting.”

options.label: Warm
options.description: “He missed the train, poor man, and went on being kind about it.”

options.label: Wry
options.description: “He missed the train with the ease of a man who had practised.”

options.label: Sardonic
options.description: “He missed the train, naturally. The universe has a sense of occasion.”

options.label: Clinical
options.description: “At 8:14 he reached the platform. The train had left at 8:12.”

options.label: Melancholic
options.description: “He missed the train, as he had missed so many things, and stood a while in the quiet.”

options.label: Wondering
options.description: “He missed the train, and in the emptied station the light fell in a way he had never stopped to see.”

fields.label: Stance note
fields.help: Anything else about the narrator's attitude. Passed to the model exactly as you write it.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Fond of the characters, never sentimental.

fields.label: Amount
fields.help: How much of the story is carried by conversation.
fields.why: More dialogue makes scenes quicker to read; less leaves room for the narrator.

options.label: Sparse
options.description: Two lines of talk, then a paragraph of narration.

options.label: Abundant
options.description: Scenes run on back-and-forth talk.

fields.label: Directness
fields.help: Whether people say what they mean.
fields.why: Subtext makes characters feel less scripted, but asks more of the reader.

options.label: Direct
options.description: “I'm angry that you didn't tell me.”

options.label: Subtext
options.description: “How nice of you to finally show up.”

fields.label: Polish
fields.help: Real-sounding speech or crafted lines.
fields.why: Naturalistic speech sounds real; crafted lines stay with the reader.

options.label: Naturalistic
options.description: “I— no, listen— what I meant was—”

options.label: Stylised
options.description: “You mistake me for a man who needs your forgiveness.”

fields.label: Voice difference
fields.help: Whether characters sound different from each other.
fields.why: Distinct voices help the reader know who is talking without tags.

options.label: Distinct
options.description: One character is clipped and formal; another rambles and jokes.

options.label: Uniform
options.description: Everyone talks in the story's own voice.

fields.label: Dialogue note
fields.help: Anything else about dialogue. Passed to the model exactly as you write it.
fields.placeholder: e.g. People interrupt each other; no speeches.

fields.label: Lens
fields.help: A habit of attention, not a subject. Write 'notices who owes whom and what things cost', not 'a story about debt'. Theme grows from what the narrator notices.
fields.placeholder: e.g. notices who owes whom and what things cost
fields.why: A lens makes the narrator keep noticing the same kind of thing, and theme grows from that.

good: notices who owes whom and what things cost
keeps track of exits and who stands near them
notices what people avoid looking at

fields.label: Genre
fields.help: A tradition or a feeling (noir, cozy mystery, space opera). It sets mood and conventions and does not require particular events.
fields.placeholder: e.g. noir, cozy mystery, space opera
fields.why: A named tradition tells the model which conventions to use and which to leave out.

good: noir
cozy mystery
melancholy space opera
avoid: a detective finds a body in chapter one

rules.message: This mentions {names}. Style travels between stories, so it should not name story people, places or objects.
rules.fix: Rephrase as a general trait of the narration, and put story-specific detail in Characters or World.

rules.message: This reads like a subject or theme. A lens works best as a habit of attention.
rules.fix: Try something like 'notices who owes whom and what things cost'.

rules.message: This asks for specific events. Genre should set mood and conventions.
rules.fix: Name a tradition or a feeling instead, like 'noir' or 'cozy mystery'.

characters.label: Character
characters.summary: One individual: who they are, what they want, how they contradict themselves and behave under pressure. It names no other people, places or objects, so it can move between projects.

groups.label: Identity
groups.help: The facts the story must never change, plus a short sketch.

groups.label: Drive
groups.help: What they want and what they avoid.

groups.label: Inner conflict
groups.help: What gets in their own way, and what they will not betray.

groups.label: Texture
groups.help: Skills, soft spots and how they talk.

groups.label: Past
groups.help: Formative background.

fields.label: Name
fields.help: What the narration calls them.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Ines Calder
fields.why: Every chapter calls them this, so pick a name you won't want to change.

fields.label: Age
fields.help: A concrete number, so the story never drifts.
fields.why: A fixed number stops the story drifting, like a 30-year-old slowly becoming 'young'.

fields.label: Sex
fields.help: Fixes pronouns and avoids contradictions.
fields.why: Sets the pronouns used in every chapter.

options.label: Female
options.description: She / her

options.label: Male
options.description: He / him

options.label: Other
options.description: They / them

fields.label: Appearance
fields.help: Concrete, checkable details: build, hair, face, distinguishing marks, usual dress. State facts, not impressions.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Tall and thin, close-cropped grey hair, a burn scar across the left wrist, always in a canvas work coat.
fields.why: If a detail isn't here, the model may invent a different one in a later chapter.

good: Tall and thin, close-cropped grey hair, a burn scar across the left wrist

fields.label: Sketch
fields.help: One or two sentences on what this person is like. Describe the person, not just a role, and if you can, include one contradiction that doesn't fit the type (a brutal enforcer who keeps bees).
fields.placeholder: e.g. A soft-spoken forger who talks to her plants when she thinks she is alone.
fields.why: The quickest way to give the model a person instead of a type.

good: A brutal enforcer who keeps bees
A soft-spoken forger who talks to her plants when she thinks she is alone

fields.label: Wants
fields.help: Two to five abstract desires that can't all be satisfied at once (succeed at school, be left alone). Nothing concrete and nobody else: aims toward a particular person live in Entanglements. The conflict between them is what drives the character.
fields.why: Wants that pull against each other are what force this character to choose and struggle.
fields.empty: No wants yet. Add at least two that pull against each other.

item_fields.label: Want
item_fields.help: One desire, in a few words.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. be left alone

good: be left alone
succeed at school
be admired

fields.label: Fear
fields.help: What they avoid or protect themselves from.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Being relied on, then failing the person who relied on them.
fields.why: Fear shows up as what the character avoids, which is easier to write than a feeling.

fields.label: Flaw
fields.help: A false belief or blind spot that sabotages what they want.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Believes asking for help creates a debt that can never be repaid.
fields.why: A flaw that works against the wants is what turns events into character.

fields.label: Values
fields.help: What they hold sacred or will not betray, phrased positively ('keeps their word even when it ruins them').
fields.why: Values give the character something to lose and lines they won't cross.
fields.empty: No values yet. What would this person never betray?

item_fields.label: Value
item_fields.help: One thing they protect, phrased positively.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. keeps their word even when it ruins them

good: keeps their word even when it ruins them

fields.label: Behaviors
fields.help: How they act in different inner states. Include at least one calm or happy state.
fields.why: Gives the model a person who acts differently as they feel differently, not one fixed mood.
fields.empty: No behaviors yet. Start with how they act when they feel at ease.

item_fields.label: When
item_fields.help: An inner or broad social state, like 'feels watched', 'is being praised' or 'is out of their depth'. Not a specific situation.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. feels watched

good: feels watched
is being praised
is out of their depth

item_fields.label: They
item_fields.help: A leaning or habit, like 'go quiet' or 'busy their hands'. Not one particular act.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. go quiet and busy their hands

good: go quiet
busy their hands

fields.label: Competence
fields.help: What they're good at.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Reads people's tells; can fix almost any mechanism.
fields.why: Knowing what they are good at lets the story reward them.

fields.label: Vulnerability
fields.help: Where they can be hurt or caught out, including shame that shapes behavior.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Ashamed of never finishing school; cannot bear being laughed at.
fields.why: Gives other characters, and the plot, something to press on.

fields.label: Speech
fields.help: How they talk: rhythm, vocabulary, what they never say.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Short, dry sentences; never says sorry.
fields.why: Lets dialogue sound like this person and not like the narrator.

fields.label: History
fields.help: Short, formative background that explains the flaw and the wants. No named people, places or objects from any story.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Raised in a boarding house where nothing was ever hers to keep.
fields.why: Explains the flaw and the wants. Keep it short or it crowds the page.

good: Raised in a boarding house where nothing was ever hers to keep
avoid: Her brother Tom left after the fire in Marlow

rules.message: This mentions {names}. A character has to work in any project, so it should not name other people, places or objects.
rules.fix: Rephrase as a trait (for example 'distrusts family'). Ties go in Entanglements and shared history in World.

rules.message: This describes a relationship to someone else. A character has to stand alone.
rules.fix: Rephrase as a trait of this person, like 'distrusts family'. Ties between people are recorded in Entanglements.

rules.message: This reads as a role, not a person.
rules.fix: Say what this person is like. A role gives the model a stereotype to fall back on.

rules.message: This gives impressions. Appearance works best as concrete details.
rules.fix: List what could be checked: build, hair, face, marks, usual dress.

rules.message: Wants needs at least two items so they can pull against each other.
rules.fix: Add a second want that pulls against the first.

rules.message: These wants don't clearly pull against each other.
rules.fix: Add a want that conflicts with the others. A suggestion can be offered for you to accept or reject.

rules.message: A value reads as a rule against something.
rules.fix: Phrase it as what they protect, like 'keeps their word even when it ruins them'.

rules.message: A 'When' box describes a specific situation.
rules.fix: Use an inner or broad social state, like 'feels watched' or 'is being praised'.

rules.message: Every state is stressful. Add a calm or happy one.
rules.fix: Add a state like 'feels at ease' or 'is among people they trust'.

rules.message: A 'They' box describes one specific act.
rules.fix: Use a habit or leaning, so a fresh version can be written each time.

world.label: World
world.summary: What exists and what is true: places, things, groups and rules. It names no characters and never says who holds, knows or wants something, so any cast can live in it.

groups.label: Overview
groups.help: The basics of the setting.

groups.label: Places
groups.help: Locations that act on the people in them.

groups.label: Things
groups.help: Objects that matter. No owner and no location.

groups.label: Groups
groups.help: Institutions, organisations, nations and crowds.

groups.label: Rules
groups.help: What is true here, what it costs, and who knows.

groups.label: Vocabulary
groups.help: Invented or local words.

fields.label: Name
fields.help: What the world or setting is called.
fields.placeholder: e.g. The Salt Coast
fields.why: The model uses it to refer to the setting the same way every time.

fields.label: Era and technology
fields.help: When it is, what people can and can't do, and the scale (a block, a city, a continent). State facts, not mood; mood belongs to Style.
fields.placeholder: e.g. A river city in the 1890s: gas lamps and telegraphs, no cars, about forty thousand people.
fields.why: Tells the model what is possible, so it doesn't invent a phone in a world without one.

good: A river city in the 1890s: gas lamps and telegraphs, no cars, about forty thousand people

fields.label: Everyday life
fields.help: What a normal day looks like for most people, and what is scarce, expensive or contested. This is the normal that Setup's disruption will break.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Most people work the docks. Fresh water is rationed and sold by the bucket.
fields.why: This is the normal the story will break. With no friction there is nothing to disrupt.

good: Most people work the docks. Fresh water is rationed and sold by the bucket.

fields.label: History
fields.help: What happened before the story that people still live with (a war, a fire, a treaty). Name no characters; anything involving specific people goes in Entanglements.
fields.placeholder: e.g. A famine ten years ago emptied the villages and filled the city.
fields.why: Gives the world weight without needing any one person in it.

good: A famine ten years ago emptied the villages and filled the city
avoid: The old king's son poisoned him in the spring of the famine

fields.label: Places
fields.help: A handful of places. Each needs a name, a concrete description, and what the place does to the people in it.
fields.why: A place that acts on people gives a scene something to push against.
fields.empty: No places yet. Add the places where scenes will happen.

item_fields.label: Name
item_fields.help: What the place is called.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. The Counting House

item_fields.label: Description
item_fields.help: A concrete description you could picture.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. A narrow brick building with barred windows and a bell above the door.

good: A narrow brick building with barred windows and a bell above the door

item_fields.label: What it does to people
item_fields.help: How the place changes the people in it ('everyone here lowers their voice'). A place that is only scenery gives the story nothing to work with.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. Everyone lowers their voice and walks on the left.

good: Everyone lowers their voice and walks on the left
Nobody stays past dusk

fields.label: Things
fields.help: A handful of objects that matter.
fields.why: A thing matters because someone wants it. This is where you say why.
fields.empty: No things yet. Add objects someone might want.

item_fields.label: Name
item_fields.help: What the thing is called.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. The Ledger

item_fields.label: Description
item_fields.help: A concrete description.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. A water-stained book bound in green cloth.

item_fields.label: Why it matters
item_fields.help: What it can do, or what it means to whoever wants it. No owner and no location; those are tracked in Entanglements.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. Whoever holds it can prove who owes the Guild money.

good: Whoever holds it can prove who owes the Guild money
avoid: It belongs to the Guild and sits in the vault

fields.label: Groups
fields.help: Institutions, organisations, nations and crowds. Say how an ordinary person meets them day to day (a tax, a curfew, a whisper).
fields.why: Groups are how the world pushes back on ordinary people.
fields.empty: No groups yet. Add who holds power over ordinary people.

item_fields.label: Name
item_fields.help: What the group is called.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. The Water Guild

item_fields.label: What it is
item_fields.help: An institution, an organisation, a nation, a crowd.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. A guild of licensed well-keepers.

item_fields.label: How it holds power
item_fields.help: Force, money, law, belief, numbers.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. Control of every well in the city, and the law that licenses them.

item_fields.label: How people feel it
item_fields.help: How an ordinary person meets it day to day. Leave out what the group wants right now; that goes in Entanglements.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. A weekly water tax, and well-keepers who check your bucket.

good: A weekly water tax
A curfew bell and the patrols that follow it
avoid: It plans to take over the harbour

fields.label: Rules
fields.help: Things that are true here. Give each a price and a consequence for breaking it; a rule with no price is just a fact.
fields.why: A rule with a price gives characters a choice, and choices are where drama comes from.
fields.empty: No rules yet. Add something that is true here and costs something.

item_fields.label: Statement
item_fields.help: What is true.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. Nobody may refuse a guest water.

item_fields.label: Cost
item_fields.help: What using or living by this rule costs.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. Hosts go thirsty in a drought.

good: Hosts go thirsty in a drought
avoid: It is just how things are

item_fields.label: Status
item_fields.help: Common knowledge: everyone knows it, and it is true. Hidden: true, but known to few. Myth: widely believed, but false. Who exactly knows is recorded in Entanglements.

options.label: Common knowledge
options.description: Everyone knows it, and it is true: the gates close at dusk.

options.label: Hidden
options.description: True, but few know it: the gates cannot be opened from outside.

options.label: Myth
options.description: Widely believed, but false: people say the river is cursed. You then say what is really true.

item_fields.label: When broken
item_fields.help: Whether breaking it is impossible, punished, shameful, or has a side effect. A hard limit and a priced choice work differently.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. Punished: the household is shunned.

good: Punished: the household is shunned
Impossible: the door will not open to a stranger refused

item_fields.label: The truth
item_fields.help: Only for a Myth: what is actually true.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. The custom was invented by the Guild to keep every door open to its collectors.

fields.label: Vocabulary
fields.help: Invented or local words and names, each with a one-line meaning, so the story stays consistent.
fields.why: Keeps invented words spelled and used the same way in every chapter.
fields.empty: No vocabulary yet. Add invented or local words.

item_fields.label: Term
item_fields.help: The word or name.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. bucketsworn

item_fields.label: Meaning
item_fields.help: One line.
item_fields.placeholder: e.g. someone who has pledged their water to the Guild

rules.message: This mentions {names}. A world has to work with any cast, so it should not name characters.
rules.fix: Rephrase as a general fact. Anything involving specific people goes in Entanglements.

rules.message: This history involves specific individuals.
rules.fix: Describe events and forces, and put anything tied to particular people in Entanglements.

rules.message: This reads as mood. Era and technology works best as facts.
rules.fix: Say what people can and can't do, and the scale. Mood belongs to Style.

rules.message: Nothing here is scarce, expensive or contested.
rules.fix: Say what people struggle for or fight over. This is the normal the story will break.

rules.message: A place only describes scenery.
rules.fix: Say what the place does to the people in it, like 'everyone here lowers their voice'.

rules.message: A thing doesn't say why it matters.
rules.fix: Say what it can do, or what it means to whoever wants it.

rules.message: A thing names an owner or a location.
rules.fix: Remove it. Who holds a thing and where it is get tracked in Entanglements.

rules.message: A group isn't felt in daily life.
rules.fix: Say how an ordinary person meets it: a tax, a curfew, a whisper.

rules.message: A group states what it wants right now.
rules.fix: Remove it. A group's present wants are tracked in Entanglements.

rules.message: A rule has no real price.
rules.fix: Add what it costs. A rule with a price gives people a choice.

rules.message: 'When broken' doesn't say what happens.
rules.fix: Say whether breaking it is impossible, punished, shameful, or has a side effect.

rules.message: A rule marked 'Myth' has no truth stated.
rules.fix: Add what is actually true. The story needs it to tell the difference.

entanglements.label: Entanglements
entanglements.summary: The live connections in this story: ties between people, who holds what, who knows what, and what is pressing on them. It changes as the story moves.

groups.label: Ties
groups.help: Directed connections between people and groups.

groups.label: Holdings
groups.help: Who holds or controls which thing or place.

groups.label: Knowledge
groups.help: Who knows, suspects or has been misled about a fact.

groups.label: Pressures
groups.help: Circumstances and agents pushing on the story.

fields.label: Ties
fields.help: How people and groups are connected. A tie points one way: how 'from' stands toward 'to'.

item_fields.label: From
item_fields.help: A character or a group.

item_fields.label: To
item_fields.help: A character or a group.

item_fields.label: Bond
item_fields.help: A standing label for the connection, which may carry a clause of shared past ('owes her since the fire').

item_fields.label: Edge
item_fields.help: A concrete aim between these two people right now: what 'from' wants from, or hides from, 'to' (wants to pass her test, hides the missing key). Abstract desires belong on the character.

fields.label: Holdings
fields.help: Who holds or controls which thing or place. Moves as things change hands.

item_fields.label: Thing or place
item_fields.help: A thing or a place from World.

item_fields.label: Held by
item_fields.help: Who holds it now. The choices depend on what it is.

fields.label: Knowledge
fields.help: Who knows, suspects or has been misled about a fact or world rule. It is measured against what is true in the story, which cannot be wrong. Someone who is simply unaware is left out.

item_fields.label: World rule
item_fields.help: A rule from World this is about.

item_fields.label: Other fact
item_fields.help: Or a short fact of your own, when it isn't a world rule.

item_fields.label: Who
item_fields.help: A character or a group.

item_fields.label: Status
item_fields.help: Knows it, suspects it, or has been misled about it.

fields.label: Pressures
fields.help: What is pressing on people, from a circumstance or from someone with their own wants.

item_fields.label: What
item_fields.help: What is pressing, and what happens if it is ignored.

item_fields.label: Agent
item_fields.help: A character or group behind it.

item_fields.label: Circumstance
item_fields.help: Or a circumstance with no one behind it, like a storm or a deadline.

item_fields.label: Agent's next move
item_fields.help: Only when an agent is behind it: what they want in this situation, not their general wants.

item_fields.label: Bears on
item_fields.help: Who it falls on: characters or groups.

rules.message: A tie goes from someone to themselves.
rules.fix: Pick a different person or group for one end.

rules.message: That holder isn't allowed for this kind of thing.
rules.fix: Pick a holder from the list offered for it.

rules.message: Give either a world rule or a fact of your own, not both or neither.
rules.fix: Fill in one of the two.

rules.message: Give either an agent or a circumstance, not both or neither.
rules.fix: Fill in one of the two.

rules.message: A pressure with an agent needs the agent's next move.
rules.fix: Say what the agent wants to do next in this situation.

rules.message: This points to something that no longer exists.
rules.fix: Pick a replacement, or remove the entry.

rules.message: This edge doesn't say what one side wants from, or hides from, the other right now.
rules.fix: Say what 'from' is after or keeping back, not just how they feel.

rules.message: A pressure doesn't say what happens if it's ignored.
rules.fix: Add the cost of doing nothing.

rules.message: A next move reads as the agent's general wants.
rules.fix: Say what they want to do in this situation.

rules.message: More than three pressures are active.
rules.fix: Let the weakest one fade or end, so the others get room.

setup.label: Setup
setup.summary: The springboard: who we follow, what just broke their normal, and what pushes them forward. It holds no plan and no ending, and it never changes during the story.

groups.label: Opening
groups.help: Who we follow and what just broke.

groups.label: Push
groups.help: What pushes them forward, and why they can't stop.

fields.label: Protagonist
fields.help: Whose eyes we follow. Exactly one, fixed for the whole story. This is the only place a character is marked as the lead.

fields.label: Normal
fields.help: An ordinary day for the protagonist before the story, drawn from World's everyday life. Say what that normal gave them (safety, status, a routine that kept a want or fear quiet), so the disruption has something to threaten. Only the first chapter uses this; later chapters carry it forward through what happened.

fields.label: Disruption
fields.help: What just broke the normal. An event, not a condition: 'the ledger went missing', not 'things are tense'. Only the first chapter uses this.

fields.label: Goal
fields.help: What the protagonist is concretely trying to do, narrowing one of their wants into this story. It can be acted on in scenes, a reader could tell whether it succeeded, failed or stopped mattering, and it costs something. During the story the current goal is worked out from this and from any redefinitions in the beats; once it is achieved or abandoned the story winds down.

fields.label: What's at stake
fields.help: What happens if they do nothing or quit. This is why they can't walk away. Tie it to a want, a value or a pressure already on the cards. It can be a friendship, a reputation or a chance at happiness, not only a loss.

fields.label: Chapter count
fields.help: A budget, not a fixed route. If the goal resolves early, the remaining chapters carry the aftermath.

rules.message: The protagonist no longer exists in Characters.
rules.fix: Pick a character.

rules.message: This doesn't name concrete people, places or routines, or what that normal gave the protagonist.
rules.fix: Describe an ordinary day, and what it gave them: safety, status, or a routine that kept a want or fear quiet.

rules.message: This describes a condition, not an event.
rules.fix: Say what happened, like 'the ledger went missing', not 'things are tense'.

rules.message: This reads like a feeling or a theme, not something to act on.
rules.fix: Say what they are concretely trying to do, like 'get the ledger back before the audit'.

rules.message: A reader couldn't tell whether this succeeded, failed or stopped mattering.
rules.fix: Make it something with a clear outcome.

rules.message: This goal doesn't connect to anything on the other cards.
rules.fix: Narrow one of the protagonist's wants into it, or add a pressure or tie that bears on it. A goal that touches nothing has nothing to collide with.

rules.message: This doesn't name a cost or a gain.
rules.fix: Say what is lost or gained if they do nothing or quit. It can be a friendship, a reputation or a chance at happiness.

rules.message: This isn't tied to a want, value or pressure already on the cards.
rules.fix: Tie it to something the protagonist wants or protects, or to a pressure.

outline.label: Outline
outline.summary: One springboard beat per chapter, planned one at a time from where the story stands. A beat is frozen while its chapter is written, and you can see the next chapter's plan before generating it.

groups.label: Beats
groups.help: One per chapter.

fields.label: Beats
fields.help: Each beat sets up a chapter: where it opens, what the protagonist is after, what stands in the way, and what they must decide.

item_fields.label: Chapter
item_fields.help: Which chapter this beat is for. Set by the system.

item_fields.label: May no longer fit
item_fields.help: Set when an earlier chapter was regenerated after this beat was planned, so this beat, its chapter and its records may be out of step. Cleared when the chapter is generated again.

item_fields.label: Where
item_fields.help: Where the chapter opens. A place from World.

item_fields.label: When
item_fields.help: The day and time the chapter opens. The scene is already in motion.

item_fields.label: Time since last chapter
item_fields.help: How long it has been. Leave blank for chapter 1.

item_fields.label: Cast
item_fields.help: Who is on stage. You pick it before planning, and the system suggests the least-used characters. The protagonist is always included.

item_fields.label: The protagonist is after
item_fields.help: What the protagonist is trying to get in this chapter.

item_fields.label: What blocks it
item_fields.help: What stands in the way. It should follow from the previous chapter's choice.

item_fields.label: Option A
item_fields.help: One side of the choice. Each option is a want or a value, and picking one costs the other.

item_fields.label: Option B
item_fields.help: The other side of the choice.

item_fields.label: Turn
item_fields.help: What is different by the end of the chapter. It is best when it pays off something set up earlier.

item_fields.label: Shift
item_fields.help: Whether this chapter makes things harder or easier. Easier is a breath, never a pause: it still changes something, and the next chapter is harder. Choices that aren't allowed right now are disabled.

item_fields.label: Ends on
item_fields.help: A conceptual stopping point that leaves a question open.

item_fields.label: Reveal
item_fields.help: A Hidden rule or a Myth from World that comes to light this chapter. A rule that has already come to light in a written chapter can't be chosen again; one that was planned but did not land can.

item_fields.label: Who learns it
item_fields.help: Which characters learn the revealed rule.

item_fields.label: Plant
item_fields.help: One thing this chapter should set up for later. Optional. It counts as open only once the chapter has actually planted it.

item_fields.label: Pay off
item_fields.help: Open plants this chapter should resolve, up to two. Optional. A plant that was planned but not written is not open.

item_fields.label: Offstage move
item_fields.help: Only when the spotlighted pressure has an agent who is not in the cast: what they did since the last chapter. The offstage pass writes it.

item_fields.label: How it reaches the protagonist
item_fields.help: How the offstage move's effects reach the protagonist this chapter.

item_fields.label: Goal change
item_fields.help: Only when the goal moves. Achieved and abandoned both end the goal, and the remaining chapters wind down with no new goal. A change that did not land in the text stays pending and is tried again.

item_fields.label: The goal now
item_fields.help: What the goal has become. Only for a redefined goal. It follows the same advice as Setup's goal: something to act on, with a clear outcome, that narrows a want.

item_fields.label: Spotlight
item_fields.help: The pressure this chapter puts in focus. The system picks it so planning stays consistent, and you can change it.

item_fields.label: Planned from
item_fields.help: A fingerprint of the live state this beat was planned from. Set by the system. If the live state changes afterward, the beat is flagged as planned from older state.

rules.message: A beat points to something that no longer exists.
rules.fix: Pick a replacement, or ask for the beat to be regenerated.

rules.message: The cast doesn't include the protagonist.
rules.fix: Add the protagonist. They are in every chapter.

rules.message: A chapter after the first needs the time since the last one.
rules.fix: Say how long it has been.

rules.message: A reveal needs the characters who learn it.
rules.fix: Pick who learns it.

rules.message: This rule has already come to light in a written chapter.
rules.fix: Pick a different rule, or leave the reveal empty.

rules.message: A payoff points at something that wasn't planted, isn't earlier, or was already paid off.
rules.fix: Pick only plants that were set up in an earlier chapter and are still open.

rules.message: An offstage move needs both what happened and how it reaches the protagonist.
rules.fix: Fill in both, or clear both.

rules.message: A redefined goal needs the new goal.
rules.fix: Say what the goal is now.

rules.message: This shift isn't allowed here.
rules.fix: Pick the other one. Pacing limits come from the chapter number and what is still open.

rules.message: The new goal reads like a feeling or a theme, not something to act on.
rules.fix: Say what the protagonist is now concretely trying to do.

rules.message: A reader couldn't tell whether the new goal succeeded, failed or stopped mattering.
rules.fix: Make it something with a clear outcome.

rules.message: The new goal doesn't connect to anything on the other cards.
rules.fix: Narrow one of the protagonist's wants into it, or tie it to a pressure or tie. A goal that touches nothing has nothing to collide with.

rules.message: An offstage move needs a pressure with an agent behind it.
rules.fix: Change the spotlight to a pressure with an agent, or clear the offstage move.

rules.message: This turn is too close to an earlier one.
rules.fix: Make something different happen.

rules.message: The turn doesn't say what is different by the end.
rules.fix: State what has changed.

rules.message: These options aren't a real choice.
rules.fix: Make each a want or a value, so picking one costs the other.

rules.message: This stopping point doesn't leave a question open.
rules.fix: End on a moment that makes the reader ask what comes next.
